title: arr.sort((a, b) => a > b) can leave an array completely unsorted
assumption: A sort comparator just needs to return something truthy when the first argument should come after the second.

input.description: A comparator written the way a boolean-returning comparison reads naturally in prose ("is a bigger than b"), instead of returning a signed number.

what_goes_wrong: In Node.js (V8), sort((a, b) => a > b) on this 9-element array returns it unchanged, [5, 3, 8, 1, 9, 2, 7, 4, 6], while the numeric comparator sort((a, b) => a - b) returns it fully sorted. No error, no warning.
why: A sort comparator must return a number: negative if a comes first, positive if b comes first, zero if either order is fine. A boolean is converted with ToNumber to 1 or 0, so this comparator can never say "a comes first". That makes it inconsistent (it reports 1 and 5 as equal but 5 and 1 as ordered), and for an inconsistent comparator the ECMAScript spec says the resulting order is implementation-defined, so what you get depends on the engine. V8's TimSort (Node.js 11+, Chrome 70+) only moves an element after a negative result; this comparator never returns one, so in V8 the whole input is treated as one already-sorted run and comes back in its original order. Older V8 versions and other engines use different algorithms and may return a partly sorted array instead, which is harder to notice in testing.
fix: Always return a signed number from a JavaScript sort comparator (a - b for numbers), never a boolean. Python's sorted()/list.sort() sidestep this entirely — Python 3 removed the old cmp= parameter and only accepts a key= function, so there is no comparator-return-type footgun to have.
